name: Rawang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: LaPolla, Randy J. & Dory Poa. 2001. Rawang Texts, with Grammatical Analysis and English Translation. Berlin: LINCOM Europa. (Mvtwang dialect; open PDF on the author's site, held)
catalog_quote: Tones are marked as follows (using the letter a as a base): high tone: á, mid tone: ā, low tone: à. All syllables that end in a stop consonant (-p, -t, -ʔ, -k) are in the high tone. Open syllables without a tone mark are unstressed. A colon marks non-basic long vowels. ... There are a number of morphophonemic processes which affect the segments and tones in connected speech. For example, when the negative mv- is added to a verb that has a vocalic prefix, the resulting form will combine the two, and it will become stressed and so given a tone, e.g. /mv-vpvt/ (NEG-give/put in) > [màpvt] "not put in". There are also often tone changes when certain suffixes, such as the reflexive/middle suffix -shì, is added to a verb.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Rawang is a register-tone language (high, mid, low on open/sonorant-final syllables; stop-final syllables are always high). Stress is not positional: every tone-bearing syllable is stressed, and the open syllables written without a tone mark — the schwa (v = [ə]) prefix syllables and particles — are unstressed and toneless. A prefix syllable that fuses with the negative mv- becomes stressed and thereby acquires a tone. In effect, in a prefix+root (sesquisyllabic) word the root syllable carries tone and stress and the prefix does not; the source does not state a syllable-count rule (e.g. 'final').
new_statements.exceptions: Morphophonemic fusion: prefix syllable fused with negative mv- becomes stressed and toned; tone changes with certain suffixes (e.g. reflexive/middle -shì). Morse 1988 (pp. 129-130) and Sarep 1996 (p. 104) independently describe the same two non-contrastive (neutral-tone) syllable classes — schwa CV prefix syllables and stop-final syllables — without using the word 'stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, stated as an orthographic/transcription convention for the Mvtwang (Mvt River) dialect, the standard written variety in Myanmar; connected-speech morphophonemics noted separately. The statement is brief (a transcription note, not a phonology chapter); the fuller primary phonology (Morse 1962, 1963) was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted material describes the Mvtwang (Matwang/Metwang, 'Mvt River') dialect of Rawang, the written standard in Kachin State, Myanmar (Glottolog language rawa1265; no separate dialect code asserted). Sarep 1996 describes the Sinwal dialect (four tonemes, falling tone instead of low), Barnard 1934 the Wvdamkong dialect, and the LaPolla 2003/2017 sketch Glottolog lists under rawa1265 is Dulong (drun1238), a closely related variety on the Chinese side.

tone_statements.citation: Powelson, Rachel. 2018. The Verb Phrase in Lungmi Rawang. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. 144 pp.
tone_statements.quote: There are four contrastive tones in Dinglak that occur on open syllables or syllables with a sonorant coda, such as /m/, /n/, or /ŋ/. These are high, mid, falling, and glottalized, as shown in Table 4. ... No contrast has been found in the tones of syllables with stop codas. ... they are usually short with a high or falling tone. ... The mid tone is used in words like /kʰē/ ‘chicken’ and /lāŋ/ ‘climb’. This tone is usually level but has a rising allotone that is used at the end of an utterance. The falling tone is used in the word /kʰê/ ‘tiger’ and /sɔ̂ŋ/ ‘love’.
tone_statements.summary: Four tonemes (high, mid, falling, glottalized) on open and sonorant-final syllables, pitch on 1-6 scale; stop-final syllables have a predictable non-contrastive tone; glottalized tone only on open syllables; sandhi unstudied; 450-item wordlist. Nothing on stress (only 'weak' half syllables in /ə/).

tone_statements.citation: Straub, Nathan. 2018. Rawang (Dvrú), Rawang (Krvngku), Rawang (Tangsar / Western Dvngsar) and Rawang (Rvmø̀l): numeral data sheets with phonological notes (data dated July 17 and August 4, 2018). In: Numeral Systems of the World's Languages, online database hosted at MPI-EVA (lingweb.eva.mpg.de/channumerals), pages Rawang-Dvru.htm, Rawang-Krvngku.htm, Rawang-Tangsar.htm, Rawang-Rvmol.htm.
tone_statements.quote: In general, however, this dialect has a similar phonemic system to Mvtwàng Rvwàng (R. Morse 1962/1963; S. Morse 1988, 1989) and Rvmø̀l Rvwàng (Straub 2016). There are three tones on syllables that do not have stop finals, based on a scale of 5 (highest) to 1 (lowest): High/rising á 35, Mid a 22~221, Low/falling à 42~31. Tone on syllables with final p/t/k or ʔ (the latter considered a tone-register complex) is non-distinctive, usually realized as high or high falling. Tone on minor syllables (Cə) is non-distinctive as well. Occasionally a distinct 55 tone will appear on certain particles, or a low-rising 24~34 tone, often associated with first person verb conjugations.
tone_statements.locator: 'Other comments' note under the contributor line (phonology paragraph beginning 'this dialect has not been fully analyzed yet')

tone_statements.translation: In the Daru dialect tone is considered to be assigned syllable by syllable. Distinctive tone appears on open syllables and on closed syllables whose coda (E) is not a stop; no distinctive tone ever appears on a closed syllable whose coda is a stop. Table 3: basic tones. Low tone /1/ [22]: pitch is low. Mid tone /2/ [33]: pitch is somewhat high, but not as high as the high tone; may fall slightly word-finally. High tone /3/ [44]: pitch is high; may fall sharply word-finally. Light (neutral) tone / / [00]: neutral accent (see below), no tone mark.
tone_statements.locator: section 4.1 基本声調 with 表3, journal p. 14; English summary p. 22 (last page)

tone_statements.citation: Morse, Stephen A. 1989. Five Rawang dialects compared plus more. In David Bradley, Eugénie J. A. Henderson & Martine Mazaudon (eds.), Prosodic Analysis and Asian Linguistics: To Honour R. K. Sprigg, 237-250. (Pacific Linguistics C-104.) Canberra: Australian National University.
tone_statements.quote: The minimal syllable exhibits as its components a nucleus plus a tone ... Every sequence of vowels, with its own inherent tone, represents a sequence of minimal syllables. A lengthened vowel or a diphthong has only one inherent tone. ... Most dialects have three tones, high (indicated by acute accent), low (indicated by grave accent) and mid (unmarked); there is also a neutral tone on some nonfinal syllables with the vowel /ə/. The Ganøng and Longmi dialects may also have a falling tone.
tone_statements.summary: Most Rawang dialects have three tones (high, low, mid) on every syllable, plus a neutral tone on some nonfinal /ə/ syllables; Ganøng and Longmi 'may also have a falling tone'. A diphthong carries one tone. Fuller phonology in R. Morse 1962, 1965. Appended 100-word list in 10 dialects is tone-marked.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number Philol 950.55)
sources.note: No use of the word 'stress'. Tones pp. 128-130: register tone language with high [55], mid [33], low [11] on non-stop-final syllables plus a fourth 'neutral, non-contrastive tone' (Morse 1962:71); 'Rawang exhibits two classes of tonally non-contrastive syllables: a) prefixal open syllables of CV-pattern in which the V is [ə]. b) closed syllables of (C)VC pattern in which the final C is a stop' (p. 130). Apparent contour tones are two coalesced vowels across a morpheme boundary.
